newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Veteran Kuwaiti MP steps aside but not out.
newsitem.headline: Veteran Kuwaiti MP steps aside but not out.

text.p: One of Kuwait's most vociferous opposition leaders is stepping aside after a long battle for the restoration of the only elected parliament in a Gulf Arab state.

Ahmad al-Khatib, known to many as "the conscience of Kuwait", is not seeking re-election in the October 7 parliamentary polls after three decades of public life although some of the reforms he strived for have not been achieved.
But the pan-Arab nationalist, left-leaning Khatib, 70, will not quit the business of politics which have led to his arrest and death threats.
"I'll always be here," Khatib told Reuters pointing at parliament's chamber. "I'll be everywhere," he added.

Khatib was the country's first Kuwaiti physician and the deputy speaker of its first elected parliament in 1963. He was a leading member among politicians who led stormy demonstrations and confrontations with the government in December 1989 and January 1990 to demand restoration of parliament which was dissolved in 1986.

The group intensified its campaign after the U.S-led coalition freed Kuwait of a seven-month Iraqi occupation in 1991. Along with Western calls for post-war reforms, Kuwait held elections for a 50-member parliament in October 1992.
"If you drop a needle you would hear it when Khatib speaks," said a fellow MP of the authority he commands. "Not many here are like such."
Nine current MPs are not running for the next parliament.

"The gap left by some of the deputies not running is hard to fill," said Mansour al-Damkhi, one of Kuwaiti's some 100,000 eligible voters. "People like them have the experience and the character that is always needed."
Hamad al-Jouan, who shares with Khatib much more than just being the only other MP who wears Western suits rather than Gulf Arab robes, is also stepping down.
Outspoken Jouan has been suffering health problems since he was confined to a wheelchair after a 1991 assassination attempt by an unidentified gunman.
Parliament's oldest member Jassem al-Saqr will not run either. Saqr, 77, enjoys a wisdom which has earned him the respect of allies and opponents alike.
He is a member of a trading family and represents in parliament a group of wealthy Kuwaiti merchants who have a traditional influential role in the country's affairs.
However many veterans are seeking re-election, making the government's dream of a more docile parliament beyond reach, deputies say.
Parliament's dignified speaker and pro-democracy campaigner Ahmad al-Saadoun is fighting a tough election battle not only to keep his seat but also the presidency.
Saadoun is reputed as a stubborn opponent known for his persistent pursuit of more parliamentary powers and keeping a falcon's eye on public funds in the oil-rich state.
Analysts say billionaire and former finance minister Jassem al-Kharafi would seek the speaker's chair if elected to the parliament which will take Kuwait into the next century.
"Kharafi would be a tough opponent. Everybody will be watching the outcome because Saadoun is not easy to defeat either," one analyst said of the two independents.

Officially there are no political parties in Kuwait which has only 700,000 citizens but liberal and Islamist candidates who differ on Kuwait's future are united in their opposition to many government policies and are keen to gain added powers.

Ahmad al-Rubai, a renowned liberal running in a pro-Islamist district, told voters: "It is important that a deputy does what he believes is right not what could please some voters at Kuwait's expense."

Before resigning as education minister in September to seek re-election, he played a key role in introducing liberal ideas in a conservative country which put him on a collision course with fellow MPs from the Islamist trend.

Hussein al-Qalaf, a Shi'ite Moslem, is probably the most controversial of the 248 candidates, with opponents accusing him of trying to use sensitive ethnic differences. Over 25 percent of Kuwaitis are of the Shi'ite branch of Islam.
